document.abstract: The capture of high-quality digital motion pictures produces extremely high data rates. The immediate interim storage of this data in realtime represents a particular technical challenge, not only because of performance requirements but also because of handling and cost constraints imposed by the production workflow. A survey was carried out to assess the viability of available storage solutions and to analyze ongoing developments in terms of performance evolution, the results of which are presented in this paper. Current and developing storage technologies are presented and their key characteristics discussed. The performance level of the different approaches is compared and, based on the research carried out, predictions are made regarding the direction and rate of future developments. The different options are analyzed as to their potential for fulfilling the demands of the storage of high-quality motion picture data, and a possible path to a technical solution is given.

authors.bio: Paul Walland holds a B.S. degree in physics from Manchester University and is a chartered member of the Institute of Physics. He is projects group manager at Snell & Wilcox in the U.K., responsible for collaborative R&D projects and is also project manager of the European MetaVision project. Prior to joining Snell & Wilcox, Walland held a number of positions leading R&D groups in the field of laser optics and optical fiber distribution systems. He holds patents in optical systems and is the author of numerous papers and review articles relating to optical networks, broadcast systems, and applications of MPEG test and measurement.
